criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban and rural drinking water supply and sanitation provision, coverage, and low-income access/affordability in Ghana (alongside agricultural irrigation water).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it examines statutory, regulatory, and institutional water sector reforms in Ghana (Act 310 of 1965, Act 522 of 1996, Act 538 of 1997, GWSC/GWCL, CWSA, PURC, WRC). Under the narrow rule-type reading, it specifically discusses tariff and cost-recovery rules (graduated metered rates, flat rates, PURC rate-setting/approval, 2% urban levy, and mandatory 5% rural community capital cost contribution) as well as utility ownership and regulatory restructuring governing water service delivery. However, these mechanisms are described only in a narrative policy overview rather than empirically evaluated.
criterion_notes.c3: No primary empirical data collection, no qualitative or quantitative empirical methodology, and not a systematic empirical synthesis. The paper is a descriptive policy and institutional overview ('Information Study') summarizing legislation, donor/agency reports, historical tariff schedules, and policy recommendations.
criterion_notes.c4: Mentions secondary macro-sector figures from government/donor reports on urban and rural water coverage (explicitly noting that 1992 and 1998/1999 coverage figures cannot be compared due to reclassification of small towns), counts of constructed boreholes/wells/latrines, and an unreferenced aggregate statement on low-income vendor water spending, but reports no empirically measured study outcome.
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design, sample, unit-of-analysis dataset, or empirical analytical evaluation linking an exposure to a household or community access outcome.

evidence_quotes.quote: This study looks at the history of water pricing, the difficulties so far encountered and the institutional reforms,

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 3 of 9 (Introduction of Water Pricing in Ghana)
evidence_quotes.quote: Under Subsection 2f of Section 2 of its establishment Act (Act 310, 1965), the GWSC has power to determine adequate rates, charges, or fees

On the average, over 60 percent of the population who are the low-income segments and who live in the rural, the fringes, and densely populated areas of urban centers have least access to water. They pay more than ten times the official rates to vendors for water supply and end up spending more than 10 percent of their income on potable water.
The communities are also required to make a contribution of 5 percent of the capital cost of providing the facility.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 6 of 9 (Water Sector Rehabilitation Project (WSRP))
evidence_quotes.quote: In spite of the improvements, water supply coverage dropped from 76 percent in 1992 to 70 percent in 1999 in the urban areas due to the transfer from 1998 of some small towns’ water supply systems to the District Assemblies and hence there was no common basis for comparison.

With the current government policy of introducing private sector partnership into the water sector the issue of tariff setting needs to be critically reviewed with the view to balance and serve the interests of the consumer and the service provider.

raw_response.exposure: Water pricing/tariff schedules, cost-recovery rules (including PURC rate regulation and 5% rural capital contribution), and institutional water sector reforms in Ghana
raw_response.outcome: Secondary descriptive sector statistics on urban/rural water coverage, constructed facilities, and vendor water affordability (no empirical study outcome evaluated)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the paper discusses Ghana's drinking water tariffs, cost-recovery rules, and regulatory/institutional reforms (passing Criterion 1 and Criterion 2 under both plain and narrow rule-type readings), it is a descriptive narrative policy and institutional overview ('Information Study') summarizing statutes, historical tariff schedules, and secondary agency reports with no empirical study design, no primary quantitative or qualitative data collection, and no systematic empirical synthesis. Decision is 'exclude' under both plain and narrow readings of Criterion 2.
